total-body-water.short: All the water in the body: about 60% of body mass in an adult. Most of it sits inside cells; the rest is around cells and in the blood.

intracellular-fluid.short: The water inside cells: about two thirds of total body water, roughly 40% of body mass.

extracellular-fluid.short: The water outside cells: the fluid bathing the cells (interstitial fluid, about 15% of body mass) plus blood plasma (about 5%).

euhydration.short: Normal body water content: the body's usual day-to-day level, which it keeps within a narrow range.

hypohydration.short: A body water deficit: less water than normal. Usually given as body mass lost, as a percentage of starting mass (2% of 70 kg is 1.4 kg). 'Dehydration' is the process of getting there.

urine-specific-gravity.short: How dense urine is compared with pure water (1.000). Concentrated urine is denser, so a higher number (say 1.025) suggests the body is keeping water.

drinking-to-thirst.short: Drinking whenever, and as much as, you feel like it, with thirst as the only cue. Also called ad libitum drinking.

planned-drinking.short: Drinking set amounts on a schedule (say 600 mL per hour), worked out beforehand from your sweat rate, to keep losses small.

sweat-rate.short: How much sweat the whole body loses per hour, in L·h⁻¹. Found from body mass before and after a session plus what you drank.

hyperhydration.short: More body water than normal, for example after drinking a lot before a race. The kidneys usually get rid of the extra within hours.

sweat-sodium-concentration.short: How much sodium each litre of sweat carries, in mmol·L⁻¹. It differs a lot between people: a 'salty sweater' loses several times more per litre than others.

eamc.short: A painful, involuntary tightening of a muscle during or just after exercise, often in the calf or thigh late in a race.

cerebral-oedema.short: Swelling of the brain from extra water moving into its cells. The skull leaves no room, so it causes headache, confusion, seizures and can kill.

hypertonic-saline.short: Salt water saltier than blood (for example 3% sodium chloride). Given into a vein, it pulls water out of swollen brain cells.

nsaid.short: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug: common painkillers such as ibuprofen, naproxen and aspirin.
